title: Operation, Simulation and Communication of Robots (winter term 2025)
subtitleHtml: Introduction to Robotics (700.820), Lecture 4 — Narendiran Anandan, Serkan Ergun. Slides from winter term 2025 (25W).
html:
The big picture

This lecture is about using a robot rather than building one. You can command it in joint space (set the joint angles: forward kinematics) or in Cartesian space (give a target x/y/z and let the controller find the angles: inverse kinematics), as positions, velocities, trajectories or forces. The four ways of operating a robot climb in autonomy: manual (a human steers continuously), teaching (a human guides once, the robot replays), programming (code, often a state machine reacting to sensors) and autonomous operation. Every mode needs limits — on joints, workspace, speed and force — and must avoid singularities. Robot parts and computers talk over communication protocols that trade speed against reliability (TCP vs UDP) or guarantee timing (fieldbuses like EtherCAT); ROS is the common middleware, built on nodes publishing and subscribing to topics. Robots are programmed in anything from blocks (Scratch/Blockly) and G-code to Python and C++, and tested first in simulation (CoppeliaSim, Gazebo, game engines). When commands come from several sources, a priority order decides — hard-wired safety first, then manual control, then automation.

Basics of robot operation

  • Forward operation: setting joint angles directly (forward kinematics).
  • Inverse operation: setting a target in x/y/z (inverse kinematics). More details later…

  • What can be commanded:

    • Target position ([x, y, z] or angle)
    • Velocity (per joint or in [x, y, z])
    • (Acceleration)
    • Trajectory: multiple waypoints (path)
    • Force / torque (depending on the type of joint)
Intuition: two languages for the same pose

Joint space: "turn joint 1 to 30°, joint 2 to −45°, …" — easy for the robot, because it maps directly to motor commands, but hard for a human to picture where the tool ends up. Cartesian space: "move the gripper to x = 0.4\,\mathrm{m}, y = 0.1\,\mathrm{m}, z = 0.2\,\mathrm{m}" — easy for a human, but the controller must first compute which joint angles achieve that (inverse kinematics). The maths for both directions is 5 Coordinate Transformation and Kinematics.

How to operate a robot?

  • Manual operation (including tele-operation)
  • Teaching
  • Programming
  • Autonomous (with or without AI)

Pictured: a teach pendant (a robot's hand-held control panel, with an emergency stop).

Manual operation

  • A user operates the robot with the control panel, a joystick or any other RC.
  • Direct control via API.
  • The robot should stop if no further input commands are given.
  • Commonly used for complex tasks with high variation of the environment.

  • Examples:

    • Cranes (forest, shipyards, …)
    • Humanoid robots with bodysuit control
    • Exploration robots (deep sea, caves)

The slide also shows a browser-based joint-control interface with one slider per joint (e.g. "J2_shoulder").

Teaching

  • Teaching is the process of manually guiding a robot — either by hand or with the control panel, joystick, RC, …
  • The robot stores the trajectory as waypoints, either manually or at certain intervals.
  • The robot is then able to "replay" the taught trajectory.
  • Commonly used in industrial applications with fixed paths.
  • E.g. welding robots.

Programmed trajectories

  • The robot is replaying trajectories that are coded in a supported programming language.
  • The robot can be programmed as a state machine to perform a set of changing pre-defined tasks.
  • Sensor readings can be used to alter the robot path (obstacle avoidance).

A state machine: from State 1, event X leads to State 2 and event Y to State 3. (Source: MDN Web Docs.)

Worked example: a pick-and-place task as a state machine

States: WAIT (no part), PICK (move to part, close gripper), PLACE (move to box, open gripper), HOME. Transitions (events):

  • WAIT → PICK when the light barrier detects a part;
  • PICK → PLACE when the gripper sensor confirms a grip;
  • PICK → WAIT when the grip fails (try again with the next part);
  • PLACE → HOME when the gripper has opened; HOME → WAIT when the home pose is reached.

Why a state machine: in each state the robot only has to react to a few specific events, and the behaviour is easy to check: you can see every path on the diagram. Adding obstacle avoidance means adding a transition such as "obstacle detected → PAUSE" from the moving states.

Common mistake: confusing teaching with manual operation

In both, a human moves the robot. The difference is what happens afterwards. Manual operation is live: the robot does exactly what the human does, now, and stops when the input stops. Teaching is recording: the human's motion is stored as waypoints, and later the robot repeats it on its own, as often as needed — that's why it fits fixed-path jobs like welding.

Boundaries & limits

  • Each joint/motor needs boundary limits for position/angle, velocity and torque/force.
  • Work envelope.
  • Prevent damage to the surroundings, humans or the robot itself.
  • Per default, self-harming robot poses are not disabled or can disabled by low-level control on mistake.
  • Singularity.
Unclear (slide 10)

The bullet "Per default, self harming robot poses are not disabled or can disabled by low-level control on mistake" is garbled. The intended point seems to be: by default, a robot does not automatically prevent poses in which it would hit itself, and such protections can be switched off by mistake in low-level control — so they must be configured and checked.

Singularity

A robot arm stretched into a singular pose, with the straight path it is meant to follow (Source: RoboDK blog, "Robot singularities").

What is a singularity, and why is it dangerous?

A singularity is a pose in which the robot loses a degree of freedom: some direction of motion of the tool becomes impossible, because two or more joint axes line up (for example two wrist axes becoming collinear, or the arm fully stretched). Near such a pose, moving the tool even slowly in a straight line can require some joints to turn extremely fast. The controller then either stops with an error or makes sudden, violent joint movements. That's why Cartesian paths are planned to stay away from singular poses.

Communication

  • TCP/IP or UDP
  • ControlNet
  • DeviceNet
  • EtherCAT
  • ROS / ROS 2
  • Many more…

TCP/IP (Ethernet or wireless) / UDP

  • TCP/IP: Transmission Control Protocol / Internet Protocol.
  • IP ensures that each package knows where to go, but doesn't care if all parts of the data arrive or in what order.
  • TCP checks if all packages are there and in the correct sequence. If a package is missing or out of order, TCP will ask to resend or rearrange the packages.
  • UDP: User Datagram Protocol — no guarantee for order/arrival, but it is much faster. It is useful when speed is important and the loss of some packages is not crucial.

TCP: slower but more reliable transfers (file transfer, web browsing, email). UDP: faster but not guaranteed ("best effort"; live streaming, online games, VoIP). Source: Spiceworks.

Why would anyone choose UDP for a robot?

For fresh data, a late packet is worse than a lost one. A camera stream or a joint-state stream at 100 Hz sends new values every 10 ms. If one packet is lost, TCP would stop everything and resend it — and by then it's already outdated, while the newer data waits behind it. UDP just delivers the next packet. TCP is the right choice where every byte must arrive: uploading a robot program, configuration files, logs.

ControlNet (fieldbus) / DeviceNet

  • Open industrial network protocols for industrial automation applications.
  • Network protocols used in the automation industry to interconnect control devices for data exchange.
  • Built-in support for fully redundant cables (ControlNet).
  • Highly deterministic and strictly scheduled.

EtherCAT (Ethernet for Control Automation Technology)

  • Open, high-performance Ethernet-based fieldbus system, primarily used in industrial automation environments for real-time control applications.
  • Fast & deterministic. Uses Ethernet hardware (LAN cables).
  • In EtherCAT, data frames are processed "on the fly". As the data frame travels through each node (device), each node reads the data addressed to it and can insert new data back into the frame in real time.

The slide's analogy: the frame is a high-speed train passing through several stations without stopping; each station quickly grabs its own mail and drops off mail for others, without the train ever stopping. (Source given on the slide: Grok, an AI chatbot.)

Intuition: why "deterministic" matters for control

A joint controller that expects a new setpoint every millisecond needs it every millisecond, not on average. Office networks are fast on average, but a packet can occasionally be delayed by other traffic. Fieldbuses like EtherCAT are built so that the timing is guaranteed (deterministic): each device gets its data at a fixed point in a fixed cycle. That's why industrial robots use them inside the machine, while TCP/UDP connect the robot to outside computers.

ROS (Robot Operating System)

  • Open-source robotics middleware.
  • More like a framework than an actual OS.
  • ROS / ROS 2 (for industrial applications, more security).
  • Allows easy communication between robots, external computers & sensors.

  • Messages (published continuously) & services (published on demand):

    • Standard data types (integer, float, double, string)
    • Special data types for sensors & actuators: GPS, LiDAR, depth camera, joint control
  • Network with one core/head/master and multiple clients.
  • A core can run on the robot or on any other (remote) processing unit.
  • Clients must be on the same network (cable, wireless).
  • A node is an executable script. Multiple nodes can run on a single unit.
  • Nodes exchange messages as "topics" (booleans, sensor data, motor control).
  • Topics are custom and use standard message types.
  • Custom message types can be created.

A publisher node registers its topic name with the ROS master; a subscriber node subscribes to that topic name and gets the publisher's information from the master; after that, messages flow directly from publisher to subscriber via the topic.

  • ROS is also used for easy communication between computers, or even between different software on the same machine.
  • Actual robotic hardware is not needed.
  • Vast online community / online documentation.
  • Last ROS 1 distro for Ubuntu 20.04 / Win 10 (Noetic Ninjemys).
  • ROS 2 distro for Ubuntu 22.04 / Win 10 (11) (Iron Irwini pictured).
Worked example: wiring an obstacle stop in ROS

Goal: the robot stops when the lidar sees something closer than 0.5 m.

  • Node 1, lidar_driver: publishes the scans on the topic /scan (a standard LiDAR message type).
  • Node 2, safety_monitor: subscribes to /scan; whenever a scan arrives, it checks the smallest distance and publishes True/False on /obstacle (a boolean message).
  • Node 3, motion_controller: subscribes to /obstacle and stops the wheels while it's True.

What the master does: only the introductions — it tells safety_monitor where /scan comes from. The data itself flows directly between nodes. Each node can run on a different computer, and replacing the lidar driver doesn't change the other two, as long as the topic name and message type stay the same.

Common mistake: "ROS is an operating system"

Despite the name, ROS runs on top of an operating system (usually Ubuntu Linux). It's middleware: a framework of tools, libraries and conventions for passing messages between programs. You install ROS on Ubuntu, not instead of it.

ROS – visualization

  • RQT Plot — plotting values (e.g. sensor signals) over time.
  • RViz — 3D visualisation of the robot and its sensor data (point clouds, camera images).
  • Gazebo — simulation (Source: automaticaddison.com).

Programming

  • Scratch / Blockly
  • G-code

  • Common programming languages:

    • Python
    • C / C++ / C#
  • Many more…

Scratch / Blockly

  • Block-based programming language developed by MIT.
  • Large library of blocks.
  • Runs on JavaScript.
  • For kids and robotics beginners.
  • Generates Python code in the background.
Unclear (slide 22)

The slide treats Scratch and Blockly as one. Scratch was developed at the MIT Media Lab; Blockly is a separate block-programming library developed by Google. It's Blockly that can generate code in text languages such as Python or JavaScript in the background; Scratch programs don't.

G-code

  • Most widely used for computer numerical control (CNC) — drilling machine, lathe, mill & 3D printer.
  • Can also be used for Cartesian robots.
  • Simple, line-based command structure.
M190  S60                       ; wait for bed temp
M109  S215                      ; wait for extruder temp
G29                             ; mesh bed leveling
G1    X10 Y-3.0 Z0.5 F6000.0
G92   E0.0
G1    X60.0 E9.0 F1000.0        ; intro line
G1    X100.0 E12.5 F1000.0      ; intro line
G92   E0.0

G-code sample for a 3D printer (Source: CNC Kitchen). List of G-code commands: https://gcodetutor.com/cnc-machine-training/cnc-g-codes.html

Worked example: reading the slide's G-code
  • M190 S60 / M109 S215: heat the bed to 60\,^\circ\mathrm{C} and the nozzle to 215\,^\circ\mathrm{C}, and wait until reached.
  • G29: measure the bed surface (mesh levelling).
  • G1 X10 Y-3.0 Z0.5 F6000.0: move in a straight line to x = 10, y = -3, z = 0.5 (mm) at feed rate 6000 mm/min.
  • G92 E0.0: declare the current extruder position as zero.
  • G1 X60.0 E9.0 F1000.0: move to x = 60 while pushing 9 mm of filament (E = extruder axis) at 1000 mm/min — the first "intro line" that primes the nozzle.

The pattern: G codes are motions and geometry settings, M codes are machine functions (heaters, fans), letters X/Y/Z/E/F are the parameters. One line = one command — which is why it suits Cartesian robots so well.

Python (recommended)

  • High-level programming language.
  • It emphasizes code readability and offers a wide range of standard libraries.
  • As opposed to C-based languages, variable types do not need to be defined, but Python is "slower" when processing large data.
  • "Programming language of engineers."
  • 521.900 Einführung in Python (Introduction to Python), at the moment German only — make some noise for English classes ☺.
Connection

"Variable types do not need to be defined" is Python's dynamic typing from 3 Variables in the programming prep course, and "slower" is the interpreted/bytecode execution from 1 Foundations of Programming.

C / C++ / C

  • C programming language family.
  • Widely used, best CPU-performing language (family).
  • Many OS and kernels rely on C.
  • Less "user friendly".

Pictured: a C++ function decoding Gray-code image patterns (OpenCV).

Simulation environments

  • Why do we need simulation environments?
  • Digital twin → digital (condition-based) monitoring and predictive maintenance.

  • Reducing costs in development:

    • Faster prototyping
    • Less need for hardware
    • Less time for experiments
    • Easy generation of training data for machine learning

Environments:

  • CoppeliaSim
  • Game engines: Unity, Unreal. Do you know any other game engines? (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_game_engines)
  • Gazebo
  • Many more…

CoppeliaSim (formerly V-REP)

  • Commercial robot simulation platform (with free educational license).
  • Allows easy integration of common robots from a library (drag & drop).
  • Advanced robot control (code and GUI) and easy sensor integration.
  • Uses Lua code; has multiple remote APIs.
  • Embedded scripts: Python & Lua (native).
  • https://www.coppeliarobotics.com/

Game engines

  • Game engines were designed for developing video games.
  • But due to their versatility, they can also be used to create simulation environments with robots, to create highly realistic scenarios.
  • Highly realistic models for collision, lighting, scenery.
  • Augmented & virtual reality (AR / VR).
  • Need high-performance computers and good GPUs.

Gazebo

  • Free & open-source robot simulation environment with full ROS compatibility.
  • Similar to game engines, optimized for robotics applications (easy integration of ROS messages and services).
Intuition: what simulation can and can't tell you

A simulated robot can crash a thousand times for free, run faster than real time, and produce endless labelled training data. But a simulation is only as good as its models: friction, sensor noise, cable stiffness and lighting are always simplified. Behaviour that works perfectly in simulation can fail on the real robot (the "sim-to-real gap"), so final tests always happen on hardware.

Order of robot control

  • We just learned that a robot can be operated in multiple ways.
  • But what happens when it receives orders from multiple sources?
  • We need to give priorities → high-level vs low-level control.
  • Safety mechanisms must have the highest priority. They are always hard-wired.
  • Direct manual operation must rule over remote or automated control.

Pictured: an emergency-stop button.

Why must safety be hard-wired rather than programmed?

Software can crash, hang, be misconfigured or be overridden by another command — exactly the situations in which an emergency stop is needed. A hard-wired e-stop physically cuts the power to the motors, so it works even if every computer has failed. Likewise, a human standing at the robot sees what's happening right now, so their direct command beats a remote operator or a program that only knows its sensors.
